passage: I am Pallavi, and I live on the third floor. Last Thursday I was at my door, watching a delivery rider, whose bag said Harsha, climb up to 3B. The man in 3B opened the door, looked at his watch and said loudly, "Three minutes late. Every time." He did not look at the rider. I could not tell what Harsha felt; his jaw was tight, but his voice stayed even. "Sorry for the wait, sir. Traffic near the flyover." He handed over the bag, said thank you, and the door shut. Harsha stood a moment on the landing, took a long breath, and tapped his phone, maybe to report it. I said, "That wasn't right." He gave me a small nod and went down.

qa.q: Which floor does Pallavi live on?
qa.a: Pallavi lives on the third floor.

qa.q: What does Harsha's tight jaw and even voice suggest about how he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he may have been hurt or annoyed but was working to stay calm. Pallavi says she could not be sure what he felt.

qa.q: What could Harsha do after such an incident?
qa.a: He can use the app's report tools, keep his dignity, and remember that the customer's rudeness says more about the customer than about him.

qa.q: How does the man in 3B seem to see Harsha in that moment?
qa.a: He seems to see Harsha only as a late delivery, since he checked his watch and did not look at him. He shows no interest in Harsha as a person.

grounding: A customer scolds a rider for being three minutes late without eye contact; the rider stays calm and reports, seen through a neighbour's eyes.
